passage:
"Sit, Reena, and listen, because your notice reminds me of mine," said Joseph. "I was twenty-five, newly working, and a letter came about my filing. I was terrified. In the corridor outside the office, a man in a neat shirt said, 'Give me five thousand in cash, no receipt, and this file disappears.' I wanted to say yes so badly.

"But something felt wrong. Why no receipt? I asked, and he laughed and said receipts were for fools. So I walked away. My uncle sent me to a chartered accountant, who filed the reply on the official portal and handed me a proper receipt.

"That man would have owned me. Next year he would have come for more, and I would have had nothing to show I was honest. Keep every receipt, beta."

qa.q: What did the man in the corridor ask Joseph to hand over?
qa.a: The man asked for five thousand in cash, with no receipt.

qa.q: What made Joseph hesitate even though Joseph badly wanted to say yes?
qa.a: Something felt wrong to Joseph, especially that there would be no receipt, so Joseph asked about it and then walked away.

qa.q: What should Reena do about the notice, based on Joseph's story?
qa.a: Go to a certified professional, reply through the official portal, and ask for a receipt for everything.

qa.q: How might the man in the corridor have seen the young Joseph?
qa.a: The man probably saw a frightened newcomer who would keep paying to make the problem vanish, an easy person to hold power over.

grounding: An agent offers to make a tax problem vanish for cash and no receipt; Joseph recognises the exploit and uses the official route.

passage:
Jomon had been sitting outside the sub-registrar's office in Ernakulam since nine, clutching the notice about his late property registration. By eleven, a woman in a crisp saree sat beside him. "Bhavna," she said. "I help people here. Give me five thousand, no receipt, and your file will be cleared by evening. No hearing, nothing."
It was tempting. His back ached. He had already lost half a day's pay.
But something felt wrong. No receipt. No name on an official list. His friend's father had once paid someone like this and got another notice six months later, and this time he'd had to explain the bribe too.
"Thank you, but I'll go through the proper way," Jomon said.
Bhavna shrugged. "Your choice. You'll wait weeks."
He did. He went to the official help desk, got a token, and, the next week, visited a certified document writer who gave him a receipt with her licence number on it.

qa.q: How much did Bhavna ask for, and with what condition?
What was Jomon feeling when Bhavna made her offer?
qa.a: He felt tempted and tired, with an aching back and half a day's pay lost, but also uneasy that something was wrong.
He refused the shortcut, used the official help desk, and hired a certified document writer who gave a receipt with a licence number.

qa.q: How might Bhavna see Jomon's refusal?
qa.a: Bhavna seems unbothered, expecting many others to pay, and uses the long wait to try to make the shortcut look attractive.

grounding: A middleman offers to make a notice vanish for an unreceipted fee; the protagonist recognises the exploit and uses official channels and certified help.

passage:
"Yash-bhai, your water connection file? I can get it approved today."
"How, Farida-ji? The officer said three weeks."
"Two thousand, cash. I know the clerk. No need to wait."
Yash hesitated. Three weeks without water at the new flat meant carrying buckets every morning.
"Will I get a receipt?"
Farida laughed. "For this? No."
"Then what happens if someone checks my file later?"
"Nobody checks."
"My cousin said that too. Then they checked." Yash's hands were cold, but he kept his voice polite. "Thank you. I'll wait for the official process."
"You'll regret it."
"Maybe. But then I don't owe anyone anything."
He walked to the counter, asked for the official timeline in writing, and paid the listed fee at the window. The clerk printed a receipt with a stamp. Yash folded it carefully into his wallet.

qa.q: How long did the officer say the approval would take?
What was Yash feeling as he refused Farida's offer?
qa.a: He felt uneasy and nervous, his hands cold, but he stayed polite and determined.

qa.q: How did Yash avoid being exploited?
qa.a: He refused the unreceipted cash offer, asked for the official timeline in writing, paid the listed fee, and kept the stamped receipt.

qa.q: How might Farida see Yash's refusal?
qa.a: Farida seems irritated, used to people paying to skip the wait, and tries to frighten him with regret.

grounding: A middleman offers a shortcut for cash without a receipt; the protagonist recognises the exploit and uses the official process and receipts.
